# Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta (MN 151 (PTS MN iii 293))
**ID:** MN 151 (PTS MN iii 293)

**Title (Pali):** Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Purification of Almsfood

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta* (MN 151) is set at the Bamboo Grove in Rājagaha [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. Observing Venerable Sāriputta's serene and glowing complexion upon emerging from evening meditation, the Buddha inquires about his practice [SuttaCentral; Emmanuel 2013; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. Sāriputta explains that he regularly dwells in the attainment of emptiness (*suññatāvihāra*), which the Buddha extols as the "abiding of a great man" (*mahāpurisa-vihāra*) [Emmanuel 2013; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Choong 1999; Yinshun, Investigations into Sunyata]. The Buddha then outlines a practical regimen of introspective reflection to ensure that a mendicant remains aloof from sensual desire and aversion during the daily almsround, thereby rendering their almsfood purified and worthy of consumption [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2010; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Yinshun, Investigations into Sunyata]. This internal review extends beyond the sense faculties to the abandonment of the five cords of sensual pleasure and the five hindrances, the full understanding of the five clinging aggregates, and the cultivation of the bodhipakkhiya-dhammas, serenity (*samatha*), and insight (*vipassanā*) [Gethin 2001; Anālayo 2010; Yinshun, Investigations into Sunyata].
According to the Pali commentary, Sāriputta's "abiding in voidness" represents the fruition attainment of arahantship (*arahattaphala-samāpatti*) directed toward the void aspect of Nibbāna [Emmanuel 2013; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Modern scholars note that the sutta's extensive enumeration of path factors and meditative attainments resembles commentarial amplification [Gethin 2001; Meisig 2010], while a linguistic study of Pali verbal morphology classifies MN 151 as linguistically late [Kingsbury 2002].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral comprise a full parallel in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (SĀ 236) and a resembling parallel in the *Ekottarikāgama* (EĀ 45.6) [SuttaCentral]. Comparative scholarship notes that SĀ 236 terms this attainment the "dhyāna abiding of the elders" (*sthavira-dhyāna-vihāra*) rather than of "great men", and lacks MN 151's opening narrative concerning Sāriputta's radiant countenance, suggesting a simpler and earlier textual stratum [Choong 1999; Yinshun, Investigations into Sunyata]. DharmaNexus aligns passages in MN 151 with SĀ (T99), EĀ (T125), the Tibetan *Abhiniṣkramaṇa-sūtra*, the *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, and the *Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali Canon, DharmaNexus detects extensive text reuse with over 50 texts, showing large shared segments with the *Anumāna Sutta* (MN 15), the *Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovāda Sutta* (MN 61), the *Cūḷasāropama Sutta* (MN 30), the Vinaya *Parivāra* (Pvr 17), and various sections of the *Aṅguttara* and *Saṁyutta Nikāyas* [DharmaNexus].
